overview: E-CoreBank is an Elixir umbrella of small apps with one-way dependencies. ecb_money and ecb_platform are the base. Reference data and the customer master (ecb_org, ecb_party, ecb_catalog) sit on them. ecb_ledger records money movements as Fineract-style journals, and ecb_branch handles teller cash on top of it. The product apps (ecb_deposits, ecb_loans, ecb_collateral) post to the ledger through the command bus. ecb_batch runs close of business, ecb_reports runs reports, ecb_events publishes business events. ecb_api_fineract exposes everything over the Fineract-compatible REST contract, ecb_api_native adds our own API later, and ecb_web is the LiveView console. ecb_migrate brings data in from an existing Fineract database. Features outside the approved scope are parked in the deferred document so nothing is lost.
implementation_order: ecb_money: pure, no dependencies, fully testable on its own. Currency, Money, rounding, day-count and interest arithmetic.
ecb_platform, part 1: command bus, command store and audit, idempotency, permissions with maker-checker, business date, configuration. The tenant registry already exists.
ecb_api_fineract skeleton: tenant header, basic authentication, `GET /offices`. The contract probe starts moving here.
ecb_org: offices, staff, currencies, codes, holidays, working days, payment types, funds. ecb_platform part 2: data tables.
ecb_party and ecb_catalog: clients, then charges, taxes, rates, interest-rate charts.
ecb_ledger: GL accounts, accounting rules, journal entries, closures; then ecb_branch (tellers and cashiers) if the pilot bank runs branches.
ecb_deposits: savings first, then fixed and recurring deposits, transfers, standing instructions.
ecb_loans: the pure schedule engine first, then products, accounts, transactions; ecb_collateral alongside.
ecb_batch: business-date roll, scheduler, loan and savings COB; ecb_reports; ecb_events.
ecb_web screens module by module as each API goes green; ecb_api_native; ecb_migrate; then the deferred features if the pilot bank asks for them.

modules.title: Money, currency and calculation primitives
modules.status: built (14 Nov 2026): Currency, Money, rounding modes, Context, DayCount and the null-safe decimal helpers; 138 tests including a 130,144-case golden master against Fineract's own Money class. Interest primitives are still to do.
modules.summary: A small pure library with no database and no clock. It defines currency and money, the rounding rules, day-count conventions and the interest arithmetic that deposits and loans both use. Every monetary value in the system passes through it, which is how we keep float arithmetic out of a ledger. It is the first module to build because everything else depends on its exactness and it can be tested completely in isolation, including against Fineract's own numbers.
responsibilities: `Money`: a `Decimal` amount with a currency and a scale taken from the currency's decimal places; arithmetic that refuses to mix currencies
Currency registry matching Fineract's `m_currency` and the per-tenant `m_organisation_currency` selection, including `decimal_places`, `currency_multiplesof` and display symbol
Rounding policy as an explicit input to every operation that rounds, never a global default hidden in a process (Fineract keeps a global rounding mode in `MoneyHelper`; ours is passed in)
Day-count conventions used by interest calculation (days in year and days in month strategies)
Interest primitives shared by savings and loans: simple and compound factors, period fractions, effective rates
Property-based tests and a golden-master suite comparing results with Fineract on generated inputs
out_of_scope: Loan schedules and savings postings: they use these primitives but live in ecb_loans and ecb_deposits
Any database access, configuration lookup or clock: callers pass everything in
Exchange-rate conversion (not part of the Fineract design we are following)
modules.api_note: This module exposes no operations. Currency endpoints (`/v1/currencies`) are served by ecb_org.
modules.data_note: This module owns no tables. The `m_currency` and `m_organisation_currency` tables are owned by ecb_org, which feeds currency definitions into this library.
modules.tests_note: No Fineract integration-test class targets this library directly. It is checked by property-based tests and by the differential runner comparing calculation results with Fineract.
design: Pure functions on immutable structs. No process state, no `Application.get_env`, no `DateTime.utc_now`
`Decimal` context is set explicitly per call (precision and rounding), because Fineract's results depend on rounding at specific steps, not only at the end
Rounding modes are an enumeration with the same names as Fineract's configuration so tenant settings map one-to-one
Every function documents which Fineract class it mirrors, so a difference can be traced to the original rule

Golden master: `parity/scripts/gen-money-golden.sh` runs Fineract's real `Money` class (from the 1.16.1 binary release) on 130,144 generated cases and writes a compressed fixture; `golden_test.exs` replays every case and requires an identical result. It covers all 7 rounding modes, 8 currencies (including 'in multiples of'), negatives, ties and 22-digit factors, and cases where the tenant rounding mode differs from the operation's

The golden master found that Decimal 2.4.1's context rounding differed from Java (its `:up` mode rounded up even when every discarded digit was zero; Decimal 3 fixed it). `ECBMoney.Precision` does significant-digit rounding and division explicitly on exact values so results never depend on a library's context implementation. Do not replace it with `Decimal.Context` without re-running the golden master
Zero has no sign: `BigDecimal` has no negative zero while `Decimal` does, so results are normalised (`-0.00` never appears)
`allocate/2` is an E-CoreBank utility that Fineract does not have; it is documented as such and covered by property tests rather than by the golden master
build_order: Currency and `Money` with scale, comparison and addition and subtraction (done)
Rounding modes and rounding helpers, with a test table taken from Fineract on inputs at every boundary (done)
Multiplication and division with explicit rounding, and allocation (done)
Day-count types and day counts (done); period fractions (next, together with the interest primitives)
Interest primitives, then the differential tests against the oracle (next)
acceptance: No function accepts or returns a float (floats raise `ArgumentError`)
Property tests: addition is commutative and associative, plus-then-minus is the identity, rounding is idempotent, allocation always sums to the original
Golden-master results match Fineract's `Money` for the generated corpus across every rounding mode (done: 130,144 of 130,144)
Interest primitives (simple and compound factors, period fractions) match Fineract for a generated corpus (not started)
open_questions: Which Fineract rounding and precision settings are tenant-configurable in practice, so we expose exactly those
Whether to publish this library on its own (it is useful outside E-CoreBank) once stable

modules.title: Platform: tenancy, security, commands, audit, business date
modules.status: in progress (14 Nov 2026). Built: tenant registry and per-tenant repos; the command pipeline (permissions, maker-checker, idempotency, stored commands with passwords masked, hooks); the read and write sides of roles (with their permissions), users (create, update, delete, change password, `{bcrypt}` hashes, password policy and reuse check), global configuration, password preferences and the maker-checker permission flags; authentication against the user table; tenant migrations generated from Fineract's schema with its seed data; the maker-checker inbox and audit trail (list, approve, reject, delete, search template; the URL Fineract records with each command), and the request handling the write side shares (Params, Validation, Changes, Integrity, RecurrenceRule). Business date is built (the feature switch, the two dates and the automatic close-of-business adjustment; `BusinessDate.current/0` gives the date to work on). Still to do: instance mode, Batch API, data tables, two-factor authentication, password reset by e-mail, sending a generated password.
modules.summary: The foundation every other module stands on. It resolves the tenant for each request or job and gives it a database, authenticates and authorises users, and runs every state-changing operation through one command pipeline that validates, checks permission and maker-checker, executes in a transaction, records the command, and guarantees idempotency. It also owns the business date, global configuration, data tables, the Batch API and the user, role and permission model. Fineract calls this slice `fineract-core`, `fineract-security`, `fineract-command*` and the `infrastructure` and `useradministration` packages of the provider.
responsibilities: Tenancy: registry, dynamic repo per tenant, per-tenant migrations, tenant resolved from the `Fineract-Platform-TenantId` header or job metadata (built)
Authentication: HTTP basic with the `/authentication` call that returns a base64 key, OAuth2 resource server, OIDC federation, two-factor
Authorisation: users, roles and permissions (`m_appuser`, `m_role`, `m_permission` with a `can_maker_checker` flag per permission); a permission check on every API
Command pipeline: command wrapper, handler registry, before/after/error hooks, command store and audit (`m_portfolio_command_source`, `m_command`)
Maker-checker: run the command, validate for real, roll back, log `Pending`; approve re-runs it under the checker
Idempotency: unique (key, action, entity); replay returns the stored result; in-flight returns HTTP 409
Business date and COB date (`m_business_date` with a `type` column), exposed through the business-date API
Global configuration (`c_configuration`, including trap-door flags), instance mode (read, write, batch roles per node)
Data tables engine: tenant-defined extension tables and entity data-table checks (`x_registered_table`, `m_entity_datatable_check`)
Batch API (several operations in one request), ad-hoc query, bulk import, templates
out_of_scope: Scheduled jobs and close of business (ecb_batch)
Hooks, webhooks and the event outbox (ecb_events)
Domain rules of any product: this module knows nothing about clients, loans or deposits
design: Command/query separation: writes are commands persisted in `m_portfolio_command_source` (columns include `action_name`, `entity_name`, `command_as_json`, `maker_id`, `checker_id`, `status`, `idempotency_key`, `result`, `result_status_code`, `client_ip`); reads are plain queries. Fineract's newer framework (`fineract-command`) adds a dispatcher, typed handlers and an `m_command` table with a `state` and approval timestamps; we follow the newer shape and keep the older table for parity

Fineract's own docs call its legacy command path 'a little bit convoluted'. Keep the behaviour (statuses, audit, maker-checker semantics) but implement it as one small pipeline: `Command` struct, `Handler` behaviour, ordered steps, an `Ecto.Multi`
Idempotency uses the header `Idempotency-Key` (the configuration default). A completed replay sets `x-served-from-cache: true`. Batch items can carry their own key
Permissions are fine-grained and per API; `can_maker_checker` marks which actions can be put under four-eyes. Roles bundle permissions

Tenant database password is never stored in the registry (a deliberate divergence from Fineract, which stores it encrypted with a master password). The registry holds the name of an environment variable
Instance roles (read, write, batch) are runtime configuration of one release, as in Fineract's `fineract.mode.*` flags; the read role may use a replica
The API is stateless; no session state on the server
Business date is a logical date separate from the calendar. Components never call the system clock for business logic; they ask the `Clock` behaviour
build_order: Tenant registry, command pipeline, authentication, read model (done)
Request handling for writes, roles, users, configuration, password preferences, maker-checker permissions (done)
Maker-checker inbox, audit trail and business date (done)
Batch API, data tables, jobs scheduler hooks
Two-factor authentication, password reset and e-mail
acceptance: A write sent twice with the same `Idempotency-Key` executes once; the second response is served from the stored result (done: tested, including eight concurrent identical requests)
A maker-checker command leaves a `Pending` entry and no data change; approval applies it exactly once (done: tested)
Cross-tenant isolation test: a command run for tenant A is invisible in tenant B's database (to do: needs a second tenant database)
The Fineract classes for authentication, roles, users, password preferences, maker-checker, global configuration, idempotency and the Batch API pass (to do: needs the API layer)
open_questions: Whether to adopt the async dispatcher variants (Disruptor, Chronicle Queue) or stay synchronous plus Oban
Password hashing: Fineract's scheme must be accepted on migration, but new hashes could use a stronger algorithm
How much of the OIDC federation chapter is in the pilot (Google federation is probably not)

modules.title: General ledger and accounting
modules.status: in progress (15 Nov 2026). Built: the accounting tables (generated from Fineract's schema: GL accounts, closures, financial-activity mappings, journal entries, accounting rules, product mappings) and the chart of accounts: list with filters, one account, the new-account template, create, update (with the hierarchy and tag rules) and delete. Also built: financial-activity mappings (list, one, template, create, update, delete) and accounting closures (list by office, one, create, comments update, delete of the latest). Also built: journal entries (manual posting of balanced debits and credits, enforcing closures, future dates, disabled and manual-entry-off accounts; reversal; the list with its filters, ordering and paging; payment details; running balances for the organisation or one office), opening balances (define and read) and the provisioning-entries list. Also built: accounting rules (list, one, template, create, update, delete) and posting by a rule. Also built: provisioning categories (list, add, change, delete) and the read side of criteria and entries. Still to do: product account mappings and product-driven postings (they arrive with the loan and savings products), provisioning criteria changes and provisioning entries (they need loan products and loans), aggregation summaries. Product-to-GL account mappings (`acc_product_mapping`) are shared by savings and, later, loan products.
modules.summary: Fineract-style accounting: the chart of GL accounts, the accounting rule that each product carries (none, cash, periodic accrual or upfront accrual), the mappings from financial activities and payment types to accounts, and the journal entries that every deposit and loan event produces. It also owns closures, manual journal entries, accrual runs and loan provisioning. This follows Fineract exactly (decision of 14 Nov 2026), with an export port reserved for a later Finacle integration.
responsibilities: GL accounts and hierarchy (`acc_gl_account`), with account types, usage (header or detail) and tags
Product accounting rules and `acc_product_mapping`: which GL account each kind of movement hits for a product
Financial activity and payment-type account mappings (`acc_gl_financial_activity_account`)
Journal entries (`acc_gl_journal_entry`) with reversal, running balances per office and organisation, and links to the originating loan, savings or client transaction
Manual journal entries, opening balances, journal-entry aggregation summaries
Closures (`acc_gl_closure`) that prevent posting before a date
Periodic accrual accounting run, provisioning criteria, categories, history and entries
A `GlExport` port with extraction state, empty until a Finacle adapter is scoped
out_of_scope: Deciding when a loan or savings event happens: the product modules raise events and call this module
The Finacle adapter itself (later)
Reports over the ledger (ecb_reports), except the trial balance tables owned here
design: A journal is posted in the same transaction as the business change, and only when the product's accounting rule is not none
Double entry is enforced by a deferred database constraint so an unbalanced journal cannot commit
`acc_gl_journal_entry` carries `loan_transaction_id`, `savings_transaction_id`, `client_transaction_id` and `share_transaction_id`, so a journal can always be traced to its cause; keep those columns
Reversal is a new journal with `reversal_id` pointing back, never an update of the original
Running balances are calculated per office and per organisation (`is_running_balance_calculated`, `office_running_balance`, `organization_running_balance`)
Accounting events are mapped by product type and financial activity; keep the mapping data-driven as Fineract does
build_order: GL accounts, tags and the account API (done)
Financial-activity and payment-type mappings
Journal entry posting service with the balance constraint, then reversal
Product account mapping and the accounting rules (cash first, then accrual)
Closures and manual entries
Provisioning criteria, categories and entries
Aggregation summaries and the trial balance
The `GlExport` port
acceptance: An unbalanced journal cannot be committed, tested at the database
Posting before the closure date is rejected
Journals for savings and loan scenarios match Fineract's on a generated corpus, line by line
The Fineract accounting and provisioning integration classes pass
open_questions: How Finacle accepts postings (API, file) and who owns that interface, needed before the export adapter
Whether the pilot bank needs accrual accounting from day one or cash accounting first

modules.title: Branch cash: tellers and cashiers
modules.summary: Cash handling at a branch: tellers (a till location within an office), cashiers who work at a teller, the cash allocated to and settled by each cashier, cashier transactions, and cash transfers between offices. Every cash movement produces journal entries, so this module sits on top of the ledger. It is separate from ecb_org because organisation data is read by everything and must not depend on the ledger, while cash handling must. Fineract keeps it in its own `fineract-branch` module for the same reason.
responsibilities: Tellers (`m_tellers`) with status and validity dates, per office
Cashiers (`m_cashiers`) assigned to tellers and staff, with working dates and full-day flags
Cash allocation to and settlement from a cashier, and the cashier's transactions and summary (`m_cashier_transactions`)
Cash transfers between offices (`m_office_transaction`)
Journal entries for every cash movement through ecb_ledger
out_of_scope: Vault and ATM cash management beyond what Fineract models
Customer-facing deposits and withdrawals (ecb_deposits); a teller records the cash side only
design: Cash allocated to a cashier and cash settled back are the two directions of one flow; the cashier summary is derived from those transactions, not stored
Each cash movement posts a journal through ecb_ledger using the financial-activity account mappings, so teller cash and the ledger never disagree
Teller and cashier validity dates are enforced on every transaction
build_order: Tellers and their validity rules
Cashiers and assignment to staff
Allocate and settle cash with journals
Cashier summary and transactions
Office-to-office cash transfers
acceptance: Allocate, settle and summary results match Fineract for generated cashier days
The cashier and teller integration classes pass
open_questions: Whether the pilot bank runs branches with tellers; if not, this module can wait

modules.title: Organisation and reference data
modules.status: in progress (14 Nov 2026). Built, and checked against responses recorded from Fineract: the read side of offices, currencies, codes and code values, payment types, working days, funds, holidays, staff and account-number formats; and the write side of offices (create, update, with the hierarchy), funds, payment types, staff, codes and code values, working days and holidays (create, update, activate, delete). responsibilities: Offices and the office hierarchy (`m_office`), office transactions
Staff (`m_staff`) and assignment of loan officers
Currencies and the tenant's selected currencies (`m_currency`, `m_organisation_currency`), feeding ecb_money
Codes and code values (`m_code`, `m_code_value`), including the system codes other modules rely on

Account number format preferences

Tellers and cashiers (ecb_branch), which post journals and so depend on ecb_ledger
design: 17 tables reference `m_office`; offices are the unit of scoping for users, clients and accounts, so the office hierarchy and the user-to-office visibility rule are implemented once here and reused everywhere
Holidays carry a rescheduling type and apply to offices; the effect on repayment dates is computed in ecb_loans from data served here

modules.title: Catalog: charges, taxes, rates, interest-rate charts
modules.status: in progress (15 Nov 2026). modules.title: Loans: products, schedules, accounts and transactions
modules.status: in progress (16 Nov 2026). Built: the loan product tables and loan products (list, one, template, create) for the core term loan; the repayment schedule engine, a port of Fineract's cumulative schedule generators for flat and declining interest, equal installments and equal principal, grace periods, daily or per-period interest, partial periods and installment rounding, with `POST /loans?command=calculateLoanSchedule` on top; and loan applications: submit (`POST /loans`), read one (with `associations`), by external id and a page of loans, approve (for a smaller amount or another disbursement date, which works the schedule out again), undo approval, reject, withdraw by the applicant and delete an application, all replaying Fineract's answers. A request for anything beyond the core (charges, several disbursements, floating rates, interest recalculation, group loans, collateral, linked savings, a fixed EMI, interest charged from a later date, repayment dates moved by a non-working day or holiday) is refused with a plain "not supported yet", never ignored. Changing a loan product or an application, and the loan template, are not built yet. Disbursement of a loan (one payout, accounting off) is built, with its transactions (disbursement and accrual) and the loan summary. Repayments (`mifos-standard-strategy`: penalties, fees, interest, principal on each installment in turn; overpaid and closed loans) are built. Undo and adjust of the most recent repayment, waive interest, write-off and undo disbursal are built. Journal entries are built for cash accounting and for accrual accounting (upfront and periodic): disbursement, accrual, repayment, waiver, write-off and their reversals, replaying Fineract's entries. A periodic accrual loan is accrued by the job "Add Periodic Accrual Transactions" (run on request through `POST /jobs/{id}?command=executeJob`; jobs are listed with their run history, and jobs without code are refused), and what is left is accrued when it is closed or overpaid. Still to do: changes to older repayments (which re-allocate the later ones), loan charges, starting jobs by their cron expression, the other scheduler jobs, and the paged transaction list.
modules.summary: The largest and highest-risk module: loan products, the repayment schedule generator, loan accounts and their whole lifecycle, transactions and the allocation of payments, charges, interest recalculation, reschedule and restructure, write-off and charge-off, delinquency, credit bureau, progressive loans and the newer working-capital loans. Fineract devotes about a third of its code to this area, so it is built around a pure schedule engine that can be tested exhaustively against the oracle.
responsibilities: Loan products (`m_product_loan` and its configurable attributes, recalculation, variable installments, borrower-cycle variations, guarantee settings)
The repayment schedule engine: equal installments and equal principal, declining balance and flat interest, interest calculation periods, grace, moratorium, multi-disbursement, variable installments
Loan accounts and lifecycle: submit, approve, disburse, undo, reject, withdraw, close, reschedule, re-age, re-amortise, contract termination
Transactions: repayment, prepayment, waive, write-off, charge-off, chargeback, refund, credit balance refund, merchant-issued refund, interest payment waiver, down payment
Payment allocation strategies (the loan transaction processor and advanced payment allocation)
Charges on loans, capitalised income, buy-down fees, interest pause
Delinquency buckets and ranges, with pausing
Progressive loan schedule model and the loan origination details
Credit bureau configuration and integration
Working-capital loans: products, accounts, amortisation, breach and near-breach, delinquency, charges and charge-off
out_of_scope: Collateral and guarantors (ecb_collateral)
Locks and close-of-business steps (ecb_batch)
Origination workflow and scoring: the core stays core
Group and JLG loans (deferred)
design: A pure schedule engine: input is the product terms plus the application, output is the list of installments (`m_loan_repayment_schedule` carries principal, interest, fee and penalty amounts, each with completed, written-off and waived components). No database and no clock inside it; Fineract itself extracted an 'embeddable schedule generator' module for the progressive model, which confirms the direction
Installment amounts are split by component and each component tracks `_completed_derived`, `_writtenoff_derived` and `_waived_derived`; keep these columns because payment allocation updates them

Payment allocation is pluggable: the loan transaction processor strategies and the advanced payment allocation rules decide how a repayment is split across principal, interest, fees and penalties and across installments. Port the strategies as data-driven rules, not hard-coded branches
Transactions are immutable with reversal and replay: a back-dated transaction triggers reprocessing of later transactions (reverse-replay). This is where most of Fineract's edge cases live

35 tables reference `m_loan`; the loan row is large and many features hang off it, so organise the Elixir code by feature context (charges, delinquency, interest pause, originators) rather than one giant module

Working-capital loans are a separate model in Fineract (their own tables, `m_wc_*`, schedule, breach and delinquency rules); build them after the progressive model and consider a separate app (open question)
Accrual and journal behaviour is per product accounting rule; every transaction type has a defined set of journal lines
build_order: Pure schedule engine for the common cases (declining balance and flat, equal installments), tested against the oracle
Loan products and the template endpoints
Loan application, approval, disbursement with the schedule persisted
Repayment with the default allocation strategy, then reversal and reverse-replay
Charges, waive, write-off, charge-off, chargeback, refunds, interest recalculation
Reschedule, re-age, re-amortise, contract termination, down payment
Delinquency, interest pause, credit bureau
Advanced payment allocation and the progressive model
Working-capital loans
acceptance: For a generated corpus of loan terms the schedule matches Fineract line by line, including rounding
For generated lifecycles with back-dated payments, reversals and charge-offs, every transaction, balance and journal matches Fineract
No unexplained diff across the whole corpus blocks the module
The loan integration classes (about 180) pass, or each failure is a recorded divergence
open_questions: Whether working-capital loans (26 tables, about 100 operations) justify their own app so ecb_loans stays reviewable
Which payment allocation strategies and interest methods the pilot bank needs, to order the work
How to treat Fineract bugs the community has fixed in later releases: follow 1.16.1 or the fix

modules.title: Collateral and guarantors
modules.summary: Collateral definitions and collateral held against clients and loans, and guarantors with their funding details and transactions. It is kept apart from loans so lending stays focused, and because collateral valuation and guarantor funding are separate concerns with their own lifecycle. Its operations are called from loan commands.
responsibilities: Collateral management definitions (`m_collateral_management`) with quality, unit type and pct to base
Client collateral and loan collateral (`m_client_collateral_management`, `m_loan_collateral_management`, `m_loan_collateral`)
Guarantors, their funding details and guarantor transactions (`m_guarantor`, `m_guarantor_funding_details`, `m_guarantor_transaction`), including hold on funds and release
Collateral value checks that loan approval and disbursement call
out_of_scope: Valuation workflow and legal perfection of security: surrounding systems
The loan itself (ecb_loans)
design: In Fineract the guarantor code lives inside the loan account package; we move it here and expose a narrow interface to ecb_loans, a deliberate improvement on its entanglement
Guarantor funding places a hold on the guarantor's savings account through ecb_deposits and releases or consumes it on loan events
build_order: Collateral management definitions and client collateral
Loan collateral and the value check
Guarantors and funding, after ecb_deposits holds exist
acceptance: Collateral value and guarantor funding rules match Fineract's responses for generated cases
The collateral and guarantor integration classes pass
open_questions: Whether the pilot bank needs collateral and guarantors at launch or after the first lending release

modules.title: Batch: scheduler, close of business, locks
modules.summary: Everything that runs on a schedule or at end of day: the job scheduler and its history, the close-of-business process built from ordered business steps with partitioned processing across worker nodes, the loan account locks that keep real-time writes consistent while COB runs, catch-up after missed days, and inline COB for a single account. Fineract implements this on Spring Batch; we use Oban.
responsibilities: Scheduled jobs and their parameters and run history (`job`, `job_parameters`, `job_run_history`, `scheduler_detail`)
COB for loans, savings and working-capital loans as ordered business steps (`m_batch_business_steps`: `job_name`, `step_name`, `step_order`)
Partitioned processing with a manager and workers; retry and resume; state kept per execution

Loan account locks (`m_loan_account_locks`: `loan_id`, `lock_owner`, `error`, `lock_placed_on_cob_business_date`, `stacktrace`), soft and hard, with bypass for repair and the orphaned-lock cleanup step
Inline COB for one loan when a real-time write meets a soft lock
COB catch-up after a missed or replayed day; business-date roll after COB
The interest-posting, accrual and similar jobs the product modules define as steps
out_of_scope: What a business step does (it lives in the product module that owns it)
The business-date model itself (ecb_platform)
design: Soft lock: COB is queued for a loan but no worker has it, so a real-time write runs an inline COB for that loan first. Hard lock: a worker holds the loan, so writes are rejected with HTTP 409. `bypass_enabled` allows repair calls on a locked loan
A lock with an error stays in place deliberately: it marks a loan that must be fixed; only locks without an error whose COB date has completed are removed by the cleanup step
COB date is derived from the business date by a strategy; transactions arriving during COB belong to the next business day
Steps are configuration, not code paths: the order is read from the business-step table so an operator can change it
Partitioned processing: a manager splits accounts into chunks and workers process them; failure of one chunk must not block others, and the run is resumable
Instance roles: only batch nodes run jobs; write and read nodes do not
build_order: Scheduler and job history on Oban
Business-date roll and the COB date strategy
Lock table and soft and hard lock behaviour
Loan COB with the standard business steps, partitioned
Inline COB and catch-up
Savings COB, then working-capital COB
Operations views: job status, locked loans
acceptance: Killing a worker mid-run and restarting completes the run without double processing
A real-time repayment during COB behaves as Fineract does for both soft and hard locks
Replaying a missed day produces the same results as running it on time
The COB, scheduler and catch-up integration classes pass
open_questions: Partition sizing and the number of worker nodes for the pilot's account volume
Whether to keep Fineract's job names so existing operational runbooks still apply

modules.title: Reports and exports
modules.summary: The report engine: stored SQL reports with parameters that operators can run and export, the standard report library Fineract ships, and report mailing jobs that run reports on a schedule and send the result. Fineract's reports are SQL stored in the database and reference its tables, which is a main reason the schema is kept compatible.
responsibilities: Report definitions and parameters (`stretchy_report`, `stretchy_report_parameter`, `stretchy_parameter`)
Running reports with permission checks, output formats and the available-exports list
The standard report library, loaded into each tenant
Report mailing jobs and their run history
Protection against SQL injection in report parameters
out_of_scope: Statutory and regulatory returns for the pilot country: a separate piece of work
Business intelligence and warehousing: consume the event stream instead
design: Reports are data: SQL text plus parameters, executed read-only. Because they name Fineract tables and columns directly, keeping the schema compatible lets the whole standard library run unchanged
Parameters are bound, never interpolated; Fineract has a dedicated SQL-injection test and we keep it
Report execution uses a read-only connection and, when configured, a read replica
build_order: Report tables and the report listing endpoints
Running a report with parameters and permissions
Export formats
Standard report library import
Report mailing jobs (after ecb_batch)
acceptance: The standard reports return the same rows as Fineract on the same data
The SQL-injection test passes: hostile parameters never alter the statement
open_questions: Whether the standard report library is imported as is, or reviewed for the pilot's needs first

modules.title: Business events, hooks, notifications
modules.summary: How the core tells the outside world what happened. Business events are written to an outbox table in the same transaction as the change and published in order, at least once, in a standard format. Hooks and webhooks call external URLs, notifications reach users, and external services (SMS gateway, email, content storage) are configured here. It is the second integration surface after the API.
responsibilities: Transactional outbox for business events (`m_external_event`: `type`, `schema`, `data`, `status`, `business_date`, `aggregate_root_id`, `category`, `idempotency_key`, `sent_at`)
Event publication with ordering and at-least-once delivery, selective producing per event type, bulk events
Event configuration (which event types are produced)
Hooks and webhooks (`m_hook` family) for events
In-app notifications (`m_notification`, `notification_generator`, `notification_mapper`)
External service configuration (`c_external_service`)
out_of_scope: SMS and email campaigns, interoperation: deferred
Consumers of the events: external systems
design: The event is stored in the same database transaction as the business change, so an event exists if and only if the change committed

Fineract serialises events as Avro, with the schema name stored beside the payload (`schema` column), and defines a standard event envelope; we follow its event types and field names so consumers written for Fineract keep working
Delivery is at least once and ordered per aggregate; consumers must be idempotent, and the `idempotency_key` column supports that
Publication runs on batch-role nodes, not on request-handling nodes
build_order: Outbox table and the write path in the command pipeline
Publisher with ordering, retry and status tracking
Event configuration API
Hooks and webhooks
Notifications
acceptance: A command that rolls back leaves no event
Killing the publisher mid-batch and restarting delivers every event at least once, in order
Event payloads for a generated scenario match Fineract's field for field
open_questions: Avro or JSON on the wire. Avro keeps existing consumers working; JSON is easier to debug
Which message channel the pilot uses (Kafka, ActiveMQ or none at first)

modules.title: Fineract-compatible REST API
modules.status: in progress (14 Nov 2026). Built: tenant resolution, HTTP basic authentication, `POST /authentication`, the read and write endpoints of offices, funds, payment types, staff, codes and code values, working days, holidays, roles, users, maker-checker inbox, audits, business date, GL accounts, financial-activity mappings, accounting closures, journal entries, accounting rules, provisioning categories, tax components and groups, charges, rates, floating rates, clients (with identifiers and family members), savings products, loan products, configurations, password preferences and permissions, the read endpoints of currencies and account-number formats, the health check, Fineract's error shapes and an HTTP 501 for operations not built yet. 33 recorded Fineract responses and 30 recorded write scenarios (about 2200 requests) are matched exactly. Contract probe against Fineract: 60 of 146 counted `must` and `should` read operations pass (41.1%, measured 16 Nov 2026 after clients).
modules.summary: The wire contract: the paths, JSON shapes, `?command=` actions, templates, pagination, error format, tenant header and authentication that existing Fineract clients and the Mifos web and mobile apps expect. It is a thin layer over the domain modules and owns no business rules. It starts in Phase 1 with authentication and `GET /offices` and grows module by module, always measured by the contract probe.
responsibilities: Routing under `/fineract-provider/api/v1/...` and `/v2/...` for every `must` and `should` operation in the inventory
Request parsing and response serialisation with Fineract's field names, date formats (arrays such as `[2009,1,1]`) and enumeration objects
The `?command=<action>` convention for state transitions and the `template` endpoints
Pagination, filtering and sorting parameters, including `pageItems` and `totalFilteredRecords`
Error responses in Fineract's format (`developerMessage`, `httpStatusCode`, `defaultUserMessage`, `errors` list)
Tenant header, authentication and idempotency header handling at the edge
A documented 'not implemented' error for every deferred operation
out_of_scope: Business rules: they live in the domain modules
Our own API design (ecb_api_native)
modules.api_note: This module serves every operation listed in the other module documents.
modules.tests_note: Verified by the contract probe over all read operations and by Fineract's whole integration suite, which drives the API.
design: A thin controller per resource that builds a command or a query and delegates; no logic in controllers
Serialisation modules per resource mirror Fineract's `serialization` packages, because the field names and shapes are the contract
The OpenAPI descriptor in `parity/inventory` is the reference; a CI job compares our generated descriptor with it for the implemented operations
Compatibility is tested, not assumed: the contract probe compares status and shape against the oracle, Fineract's own tests compare behaviour
build_order: Tenant header, authentication, error format, `GET /offices` (done)
Read endpoints of the reference data and administration resources (done)
Write endpoints of the organisation and administration resources, through the command pipeline (done)
Maker-checker inbox, then clients and catalog resources (next)
Deposits resources, then loans resources
Accounting, reports, hooks and the remaining `must` operations
The `should` operations; the deferred operations return 'not implemented'
acceptance: Contract probe pass rate rises monotonically and reaches 100% of counted `must` read operations (now 20 of 146)
Fineract's integration suite pass rate per module meets that module's acceptance criteria
The stock Mifos web app logs in and browses every implemented area
open_questions: How to handle the version gap: the latest Mifos web app targets Fineract 1.14 while the contract is 1.16.1

modules.title: Native E-CoreBank API
modules.status: not started (after the compatible API is stable)
modules.summary: Our own API under `/api/ecb/v1`, designed for new clients rather than for compatibility. It exists because the Fineract contract has quirks that we keep for parity but would not choose today. It calls the same domain modules and the same command pipeline, so there is one set of business rules behind both APIs.
responsibilities: A cleaner resource model with consistent pagination, ISO date strings and standard error objects
OpenAPI-first definition with generated documentation
The same authentication, tenant resolution, idempotency and maker-checker as the compatible API
out_of_scope: Duplicating business logic: it only adapts
modules.api_note: No operations yet; they are defined in an ADR when this module starts.
modules.tests_note: No Fineract test class applies: this API has no Fineract counterpart.
design: Both APIs go through the same commands; a rule fixed once is fixed for both
Versioned from the start, with the backward-compatibility check Fineract applies to its own API
build_order: ADR with the resource model, after the compatible API covers clients, deposits and loans
Read resources first, then commands

modules.title: LiveView console (the Mifos rewrite)
modules.status: Phoenix shell exists; no console screens

Until a screen exists the stock Mifos web app can run against the compatible API, so there is always a usable console while this one is built.
responsibilities: A design system: tables, forms, wizards, detail tabs, search, the maker-checker inbox
Screens per area, in the order of the module build: organisation, clients, deposits, loans, accounting, administration
Login, tenant selection, permission-aware navigation
Dashboards and operational views (job status, locked loans, pending approvals)
out_of_scope: The mobile apps and customer self-service: API clients, kept as they are
Business rules: the console calls the same command and query layers as the API
modules.api_note: This module serves screens, not API operations.
modules.tests_note: No Fineract test class applies. Screens are checked against the Mifos web app's flows with recorded browser tests.

modules.title: Migration from an existing Fineract database
modules.summary: A tool that brings an existing Fineract tenant into E-CoreBank. Because the schema follows Fineract's, migration is a verified data copy, plus the pieces that differ: the tenant registry entry, password handling and any version skew. It also produces a reconciliation report so a bank can prove nothing was lost.
responsibilities: Create a tenant database from our migrations and copy data table by table in dependency order
Handle schema version skew by reading Fineract's Liquibase history
Convert tenant connection details into a registry entry (no password stored)
Reconciliation: row counts, sums of balances and journals, and per-account checks
Dry run, resume after failure, and a cutover runbook
out_of_scope: Migration from systems other than Fineract
modules.api_note: This module exposes no API; it is a command-line tool.
modules.data_note: This module owns no tables. It reads a Fineract database and writes ours.
modules.tests_note: No Fineract test class applies. It is tested by migrating the oracle's own database and comparing the result.
design: Fineract moved from Flyway to Liquibase at 1.7 and refuses to start on a database older than 1.6; the tool applies the same rule and states the supported source versions
Money and balances are compared by exact decimal equality, never by float
The oracle itself is the test bed: migrate it and run the contract suite against the migrated copy
build_order: Schema version detection and the supported-version rule
Table copy in dependency order, with the reconciliation report
Dry run, resume, cutover runbook
Rehearsal on the oracle database
acceptance: A migrated oracle database passes the same contract checks as the oracle
Reconciliation shows zero differences in counts and balance totals
open_questions: Which Fineract versions the pilot bank might be migrating from

modules.title: Deferred features (not built in the first releases)
modules.status: parked by the cut list approved on 14 Nov 2026
modules.summary: Features in Fineract that a retail bank rarely needs and that the approved cut list parks: group and centre lending, meetings and calendars, collection sheets, share accounts and products, survey and poverty-index scorecards, the investor module for selling loan portions, SMS and email campaigns, and interoperation. Each deferred endpoint returns a documented 'not implemented' error and shows as skipped in the contract suite. This document keeps the scope, tables and tests together so any of them can be revived without rediscovery.
responsibilities: Nothing is built. This document is the record of what exists in Fineract and what reviving each feature would take

The investor module (asset externalisation) is event- and COB-driven and touches loans and accounting; it needs ecb_events and ecb_batch first
If any of these is revived it becomes its own app with its own document, not an addition to an existing module
build_order: Not scheduled. Estimate and schedule only when a pilot bank asks
acceptance: Every deferred operation returns the documented 'not implemented' error
The contract suite marks the corresponding classes skipped, with the reason

excluded_packages.client: Generated and hand-written Java SDK clients (fineract-client, fineract-client-feign). Not server code: E-CoreBank has no need for a Java client.
